A release has two steps. First we upload every new asset under a versioned name, so the new files sit beside the current ones without replacing anything. Then we switch the manifest to point at those new names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never points at a file that isn't there yet. If we switched first, any browser that fetched the new manifest before the upload finished would request missing assets and get a broken page. Uploading first means the switch takes effect all at once and every name it references already exists.

We keep the old assets because some browsers have already loaded the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it names. Deleting those files would break pages that are already open or cached. Since each version has its own names, the old and new assets can safely coexist.

A release has two steps: we upload every new asset under a versioned name, then we switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that isn't there yet. As soon as the manifest switches, browsers start requesting the names it lists. If we switched first, those requests could hit missing files and the page would break until the upload caught up. Because the new names are versioned, uploading them early doesn't touch anything the live manifest uses, so it's safe to do while the old release is still serving.

We keep the old assets because some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and will keep requesting the old names it listed. If we deleted those files at the switch, those browsers would get failures partway through loading. Leaving the old versions in place lets both manifests resolve completely, so the switch is safe for everyone, whichever manifest they loaded.
